name: Lena Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for a side. What you tell me is confidential. Can you take me through an ordinary workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Lena Costa, twenty-seven, and I lead three accountants at Vale Street Tax. I have a master's and a chartered accountancy qualification, but the pay is low for the work. I open bank feeds, review tax returns, and sit with small charity clients who need someone to explain a number without making them feel stupid.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part do you like, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the client clinic because someone walks out knowing what their bills mean. I use AI tools daily for first drafts and checks, though I sign off after checking the source. Rent eats my pay, I have less than one month saved, and there are few similar jobs nearby. The team comes to me for answers, but I sometimes go home with my own questions unanswered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small improvement would be welcome. The tool I use now catches dull mistakes in draft tax letters, but I still check every figure against the source file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the junior accountants to use the tool and show their workings. I'd tell clients that a faster draft doesn't mean they can skip the fee for a qualified person to sign it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel foolish for racing to learn every new release, but I wouldn't stop. I lead three people at Vale Street Tax, and our partners already ask why a machine can't do the first pass. My pay is low for a chartered accountant with a master's, and I have less than one month's expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my weekly review meeting and the existing client list. This month I'd ask the partners for a modest raise using our return times, then move fifty a month from takeaway meals into savings if they agree. I'd keep using AI daily for draft letters, with a person checking the numbers. If they refuse, I'll save twenty a month instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little relieved about the work, still tight in the chest about rent. There are few accounting firms close enough to commute to, so a bad month at Vale Street matters even without a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the money pressure look like in an ordinary month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My rent rose again in September, and I covered it by leaving the dentist appointment for later. Small AI time savings won't pay for the dentist appointment I've postponed. I'd book it after two months of a higher wage, not on hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the partners refuse the raise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the return log to Mira, the managing partner, and ask for a number rather than praise. If she says no, I'll still save something, probably twenty a month. I won't pretend a new app pays my rent.

say: I would call **AI** a useful check on routine drafts.
I would still tell clients a **qualified accountant** owns the final tax return.
think: My **low pay** hurts more than the software in this picture.
I fear a weak month because **nearby jobs** are scarce.
do: Keep the **weekly review** and check AI drafts against source files.
Ask the partners for a **raise** using return times.
Save **fifty monthly** if the raise comes, or twenty if refused.
feel: I feel **relieved** about the work but worried about rent.
S0.quote: Small AI time savings won't pay for the dentist appointment I've postponed.
fieldNote: A **strained budget** persists even when Lena expects her accounting role to remain.
Daily **AI use** continues with human checks before tax returns leave the firm.

steps.text: Keep weekly reviews and check AI tax letters against source files
Save fifty monthly if raise granted, twenty otherwise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is closer to what I see on my screen already. The bank feed now sorts most entries before anyone opens the file, although it still mislabels the odd payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should make the saved hours visible and share them, maybe with shorter weeks. To friends I'd say I want staff at the table before a partner decides three juniors have become one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be the last accountant in my team rather than the first one fired. That isn't much comfort when I trained two of them. My client calls and judgment may last longer, but returns, checking and letters fill most of my actual day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the next month I'd log which errors the bank-feed tool makes and train my team to spot them. I'd take the figures to our staff association and ask for a written rule on redeployment before any vacancies are frozen. If the partners reject that, I'd apply to the hospital trust's finance office, though openings there are rare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because I can see my team getting smaller before my own title changes. I can act, but a spreadsheet won't protect three salaries by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which colleague comes to mind first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jon, my newest colleague, has just signed a lease near the office. I'd tell him to keep evidence of the client issues he solves, not just the number of returns he finishes. We could use that in a meeting about roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put to the managing partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mira for the error rate, the hours saved and a date for discussing jobs. If I only ask for a promise, she'll give one and the next vacancy will quietly disappear. I want our staff association at the meeting where partners decide which accounting jobs disappear.

say: I would ask for **shared savings** from faster accounts.
I would insist staff discuss **vacancies** before roles vanish.
think: My **lead role** may survive while junior posts shrink.
Client calls help, but **routine returns** occupy most days.
do: Log **bank-feed errors** and teach the team to catch them.
Bring **vacancy data** to the staff association.
Apply to the **hospital finance office** if the partners refuse a jobs agreement.
feel: I feel **anxious** for my team and my own income.
S1.quote: I want our staff association at the meeting where partners decide which accounting jobs disappear.
fieldNote: Faster **bank feeds** point directly to fewer junior vacancies at Vale Street.
Her **outside application** depends on a rejected staff agreement and a rare local opening.

steps.text: Train three colleagues to catch bank-feed errors in tax files
Ask staff association to negotiate vacancy and redeployment rules
Apply to hospital finance office if partners reject jobs agreement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is barely two tax seasons. If the software can do almost all thinking work more cheaply by 2028, our neat job titles won't mean much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that the government needs wage support and rules before firms start cutting. At Vale Street I'd ask for open books on what the partners plan to automate, because staff can't plan around rumours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could lose this job in the first year after 2028, even if I become the best person at using the system. Most of my work is on a screen; robots arriving around 2031 don't give me extra time. With less than a month's cushion, I'd be asking my sister for a sofa before I found another local accounting post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start this week by cancelling my annual travel subscription and saving the sixty a month. I'd put in applications for public service finance roles now, while a vacancy still exists, and ask my sister whether I could stay for a month if income stopped. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for any wage support available and use any payment for rent while I looked beyond accountancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm frightened, and I don't have a clever business answer. I can make calls today, but I can't manufacture an extra year of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually ask your sister?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sister Amara that the sofa is a backup, not a plan for her to feed me. She works shifts at a pharmacy and has her own bills. Asking her would be my last move after the rent account ran dry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which expense goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first bill I'd protect is rent, then electricity. I'd stop the travel subscription now, not after I got a notice. I wouldn't take a costly course just because someone says reskilling fixes everything.

say: I would demand **wage support** before accounting jobs disappear.
I would ask Vale Street to publish its **automation plan**.
think: I expect my **screen-based job** to go soon after 2028.
My **thin cushion** could force me onto my sister’s sofa.
do: Cancel the **travel subscription** and save sixty monthly.
Apply now for **public finance vacancies** beyond Vale Street.
Ask my **sister** about emergency lodging; seek wage support after 2028 to cover rent while searching beyond accounting.
feel: I feel **frightened** by job loss and a rent deadline.
S2.quote: I can't manufacture an extra year of rent.
fieldNote: **Thinking AI** reaches her desk work in 2028; later robots give her no extra time.
Her **sister’s sofa** is a last resort because Amara has bills of her own.

steps.text: Cancel annual travel subscription and save sixty each month
Apply for public service finance vacancies before 2028
Ask sister Amara about one month of emergency lodging
Apply for available wage support after 2028 while seeking work beyond accounting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives us a few budget cycles. That is time to bargain and learn, if we use it instead of congratulating ourselves for having time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firm should publish a path for staff to move into client advice and checking automated work. I'd ask the accountants' association to press for paid training, because the partners get the savings first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might still lose my present job after 2031, because most tax preparation is thinking work. But five years could let me become a financial adviser for small charities, with work that includes hard conversations people may still want from a person. The robots around 2034 don't change my desk-work deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd enrol in the four-hundred charity finance course if Vale Street pays the fee. I'd shadow our adviser on Friday mornings if Mira approves paid release from the return queue. I'd ask the association to bargain for those paid hours before roles are cut. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if my tax role ends, I'd apply for a funded charity advice post that pays my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can picture a route with dates and names. It is not a guarantee; I still have rent every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The course is four hundred. I can't pay that upfront while my account is this thin, so I'd ask Vale Street for the training budget in writing. If they refuse, I'll use free lectures and keep applying elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the new path is real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give myself a year to see whether the adviser can actually hand me client cases. If the course is only a certificate on my wall, I will not call it a new career. I'd ask clients what help they still pay for.

say: I would ask for **paid training** before 2031.
I would demand a clear **staff path** into advice work.
think: My current **tax role** is exposed when AGI arrives.
Five years could buy me a **charity advice** role.
do: Enrol in the **four-hundred course** if Vale Street pays; otherwise use free lectures and keep applying elsewhere.
Shadow the **client adviser** on Fridays if Mira approves paid release.
Ask the **association** for paid hours; apply for a funded advice post after 2031 if tax work ends.
feel: I feel **worried**, though I can see a route.
S3.quote: If the course is only a certificate on my wall, I will not call it a new career.
fieldNote: **Firm funding** and paid release make study possible without taking on debt.
Real **client cases** will test whether her proposed advice path has substance and a paying employer.

steps.text: Take charity finance course if firm pays fee; otherwise use free lectures
Shadow client adviser Fridays if Mira grants paid release
Ask accountants association to bargain for paid transition hours
Apply for funded charity advice post after 2031 if pay covers rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years sounds generous until you remember how long a career takes to build. I'd be thirty-seven, and I could have become useful in a different part of finance by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should use the decade to shorten hours without cutting wages as returns get faster. I'd also argue for public training places, because a worker in a small firm can't fund ten years of reinvention alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still expect routine accounting to be hollowed out when AGI comes in 2036. But I could move toward helping community organisations decide what to do with their money, while they still trust a human in the room. The robots arriving about 2039 don't change that timing for my desk work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd keep the monthly client clinic I started for our smallest charities and record which questions need human judgment. I'd put forty a month into an emergency account before paying for courses. Next spring I'd ask the local community foundation about paid finance adviser vacancies; I'd move only if there is an actual post and a wage I can live on. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, if my tax role ends, I'd apply for a funded foundation vacancy only if its salary covers rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with some room to breathe. My rent is still high, but I can make ten small decisions rather than one desperate leap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in that client clinic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the clinic, a youth club treasurer wanted to know whether a grant would cover winter heat. The tool could recite the rules, but I sat with her through the cash flow. I'd keep doing that work while anyone pays for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the foundation move possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The foundation would need a funded vacancy and a salary that covers rent; I won't jump for a title alone. If no post opens, I'll keep the clinic and the savings account going. Ten years only helps if I use each year.

say: I would seek **shorter hours** from productivity gains in our tax team.
I would back **public training** for small-firm workers.
think: Routine **tax work** still shrinks by 2036, including the reviews I lead.
A **community finance** role might give me a better landing.
do: Keep the **monthly clinic** for small charity clients.
Save **forty monthly** before paying for courses.
Ask about a **funded foundation vacancy**, then apply after 2036 if pay covers rent.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, but I have time to build options.
S4.quote: Ten years only helps if I use each year.
fieldNote: The **client clinic** helps her test demand while a small cash reserve grows.
A **foundation move** requires a funded opening and a salary that covers rent.

steps.text: Keep monthly finance clinic for smallest charity clients
Save forty monthly in an emergency account
Apply for funded foundation adviser vacancy after 2036 if salary covers rent

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. My desk work is hit when the thinking system arrives, and two years isn't enough to build a cushion from this pay. A year of wage support, open plans from the firm, and paid training tied to real vacancies would help. My sister's sofa cannot be the country's employment plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets the hours we save now, before full AGI. If three people produce the same returns in half the time, a shorter week could be a real benefit. If the partners just stop replacing people, the savings will look good on paper and feel terrible in this room.

headlineQuote: My sister's sofa cannot be the country's employment plan.
portrait: At **twenty-seven**, Lena leads three accountants and prepares returns for small charities at Vale Street Tax.
She has a **master’s** and chartered qualification, yet low pay leaves less than one month of savings.
She uses **AI daily**, checks its work, and presses for staff to share saved hours.
Few **nearby jobs** make the 2028 shock frightening; longer timelines let her test charity finance work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens her screen-based job before she can build a cash cushion.
whatWouldHelp: She asks for **wage support**, open firm plans, and paid training linked to actual vacancies.
